What counts as climate-tax in WA: Climate Commitment Act (CCA)
•The main policy is the CCA, a “cap-and-invest” program passed in 2021.  
•Under the CCA, large emitters of greenhouse gases (e.g., power plants, refineries, big industry) must buy “allowances” for each metric ton of CO₂ (or equivalent) they release.  
•The total number of allowances is gradually reduced over time (“cap”), forcing polluters to cut emissions or pay for allowances; over time this should reduce emissions significantly.  

💲 What the “tax” looks like in practice
•Although the CCA doesn’t directly tax retail fuel or electricity, the increased cost to businesses tends to be passed on to consumers — so many people feel a resulting “climate-tax effect.”  
•As of recent allowance auctions, prices have been rising: e.g. one recent auction settled at about $50 per metric ton CO₂, up from earlier values.  
•Those allowance prices are often translated into approximate impacts on gasoline and diesel prices: for example, one analysis put the cost of the CO₂ tax at around $0.46 per gallon of gasoline, or $0.56 per gallon of diesel at that time.  
•In 2023, a typical price was estimated around $54.74 per metric ton, equating to roughly $0.43 per gallon of gas (and $0.53/gal diesel).  

🏛️ What the tax revenue gets used for

The state does not just collect the money — a core feature of the CCA is reinvestment:  
•Over the 2023–2025 biennium, the state invested over $1.5 billion of CCA revenue.  
•According to the state, more than $330 million of that is expected to directly reduce greenhouse gas emissions — at a calculated cost of roughly $40 per metric ton of CO₂ reduced.  
•Other spending goes to climate resilience, clean-energy infrastructure (e.g. EV charging, clean transit), air-quality improvements, community health and, in many cases, targeting more vulnerable or overburdened communities.  

📉 What’s been the political / public reaction & recent developments
•In November 2024, voters in Washington rejected Initiative 2117 — a proposed repeal of the CCA program.  
•After the repeal effort failed, allowance prices increased significantly — which supporters say restores stability in the carbon market and ensures continued revenue for climate programs.  
•However, critics argue the CCA (or “CO₂ tax,” as some call it) has added to energy and fuel costs for households, especially as allowance prices rise.
